Start your day with a shot of inspiration from your favourite speakers. Expect stimulating ideas along with fresh pastries and coffee.

Modern science buries its assumptions. One of continental philosophy's most uncompromising voices, Babette Babich, digs them up. Drawing on Nietzsche, Heidegger, and Adorno, join her to interrogate what analytic thinking consistently fails to see in science, technology, philosophy, and digital culture.

events.title: Philosophy Breakfast with Babette Babich

Start your day with a shot of inspiration from your favourite speakers. Expect stimulating ideas along with fresh pastries and coffee.

God is back in politics, and the New Right put him there. Join former communist turned radical moderate, Orwell Prize-winning journalist David Aaronovitch, to trace how Christian nationalism is being weaponised across the West.

events.description:
Science has mapped galaxies and genomes, yet consciousness remains elusive. Join physicist and astronomer, Adam Frank, as he calls out science’s biggest blind spot. The problem is not data, but perspective. Treating mind as a side effect leaves experience unexplained. Frank urges a new approach where consciousness is integral to reality's nature, not something that emerges from physical matter. To move forward, science must confront the mystery of consciousness itself, not just examine the equations that play in its shadows.

"With wit and brio, Frank separates current nonsense... from the serious." – Carlo Rovelli
events.title: Consciousness is Science's Blind Spot

events.description:
Across the Western world, populism has been on the rise and is transforming politics. In this two-part course, Frank Furedi, Emeritus Professor of Sociology and one of the most widely cited social commentators in the UK press, explores what populism really consists of, why it is so frequently dismissed, and what its future is likely going to be. Furedi reframes populism as a democratic disposition: a genuine demand for solidarity, cultural security, and the right to be heard. Now director of the Hungarian think tank MCC Brussels, Furedi argues that the world must take populism seriously and engage with its underlying philosophy on its own terms.

Part 1: The anti-populist narrative: A brief history of populism - from its roots in Ancient Greece to the modern anti-populist narrative.

Part 2: Populism as a democratic disposition: Far from being a threat to democracy, Furedi makes the case that populism may be one of its most authentic expressions.

"Furedi's analysis is brilliant." – Jonathan Haidt
events.title: The History and Philosophy of Populism

events.description:
Would you trade your data for a healthier or fairer society? Every time you visit a doctor, enrol a child in school, or interact with a public service, you generate a record. For decades, this data sat in silos – collected to run services, never joined up. Now it can be linked at scale, revealing patterns in public health and inequality that were previously invisible. Join Dr Emma Gordon, director of the £168m Administrative Data Research UK programme, as she makes the case that the data trail of everyday life could transform how we understand and improve public services.

In partnership with ADR UK
events.title: Big Data Matters

events.description:
The scientific revolution, from Copernicus to Newton, made science the winner in the race to uncover the ultimate nature of reality. But a hundred years ago, Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle and the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics undermined that vision, placing reality beyond the reach of physics. Despite the theory's remarkable predictive success, from the outset many refused to accept this outcome. Einstein famously declared, "God does not play dice" with the universe. Seeking to hold onto reality, some have put forward an uncountable infinity of parallel universes while others propose mysterious hidden variables. Critics argue these notions are driven not by evidence but by the emotional desire to believe in a describable reality, since the Copenhagen interpretation is precisely accurate, to 12 decimal places, in its predictions.

Should we accept the view that science’s ambition to reveal reality was always an illusion? And see alternatives as driven by the desire to retain ultimate truth? Or was Einstein right to insist that science needs to maintain the ability to provide a God's eye view of reality?

Former Editor of Nature Philip Ball, author of Beyond the Quantum, physicist Antony Valentini, and theoretical physicist and YouTuber Sabine Hossenfelder debate quantum physics and reality.
events.speakers: Philip Ball, Antony Valentini, Sabine Hossenfelder. Bjorn Ekeberg hosts
events.title: Lost in the Quantum World

events.description:
Trump aside, many imagine free trade is clearly the best economic strategy. Nations that opened their borders grew wealthy, those that closed stagnated. But the evidence tells a more complicated story. America became the wealthiest country in the world behind tariff walls that averaged over 40% during its industrial rise. The European Union — cheered on as a liberal success story — is seen as a highly protectionist bloc by emerging countries, with some dairy, meat, and sugar products having tariffs over 100%. Meanwhile, South Korea didn't build Hyundai and Samsung by trusting the market — the government backed handpicked industries, and blocked foreign competitors. China did the same.

Should we stop thinking of free trade as automatically a good thing and recognise that protectionism is sometimes essential for growth? Is free trade only effective when a country is economically dominant, as Britain was in the 19th century, and the US post WWII? Or has free trade been responsible in the last 70 years for the fastest rise in living standards the world has ever seen, which we abandon at great peril?

Former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt, heterodox economist Steve Keen, member of the FT editorial board Gillian Tett, and FT Chief Economics Commentator Martin Wolf debate free trade, tariffs, and dogma in economics.
events.speakers: Steve Keen, Jeremy Hunt, Gillian Tett, Martin Wolf. Hilary Lawson hosts
events.title: The Central Dogma of Economics

events.description:
Philosophers, neuroscientists, and mystics alike have spent decades or even centuries attempting to locate the self. None have ever found it. Join Hegelian philosopher Sebastian Rödl as he argues the self has not yet been found for a very peculiar reason. The self is not an object in the world. Rather, Rödl argues, the self provides the very possibility for knowing or experiencing a world at all.

"Incredibly ambitious." – Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews
events.title: The Self Is Not In The World

events.description:
Michael Gove has spent his career reforming the institutions he served, from schools to Whitehall to the heart of the Conservative Party. A journalist turned senior Cabinet Minister, a leading figure in the Brexit campaign, and now editor of The Spectator, he has long believed that the status quo must always be questioned — even from within. But what are the philosophical ideas and values that have been the drive behind his influence and controversial career, and what life experiences shaped them? Join Michael Gove as he reflects on the ideas, gambles and experiences behind a life spent at the collision point of thought and power. Interviewed by Mary Ann Sieghart.

"Michael is the dominant orator of our generation." – Nick Boles

In partnership with The Spectator
events.title: The Life and Philosophy of Michael Gove

events.description: A speedy mouse peeks out of his hole, whilst a hungry cat waits silently around the corner. But before either of them makes a move, can you know who's going to win the chase? Join philosopher Peter Worley in a game of Cat & Mouse, exploring whether you can predict the future or if it's all chance. Can you spot the important clues, or will the outcome surprise everyone?
events.title: The Great Cat and Mouse Chase

events.description:
Sage & Jester presents
Louis Theroux on the cult of the online
in conversation with Robin Clyfan

Genre-defining documentary filmmaker and presenter Louis Theroux is best known for his immersive and empathetic programmes exploring the intricate and often contentious facets of human experience.
He’s spent thirty years trying to understand the kinds of extremists others would easily write off - always responding with curiosity rather than judgement. Few people have studied so closely how people get pulled in, and what it takes to get out.

In this exclusive, one-off event, we'll be asking him to turn that same eye on all of us, to ask, with trademark Louis curiosity: have we all been collectively groomed into the cult of the online? Which cult-like behaviours are we already exhibiting in how we scroll, argue, believe, and belong? And how do we think our way out of them?

Expect the same scrutiny turned on the cult of productivity - the pressure to optimise everything, and what that quietly costs us in reflection, empathy, and the freedom to simply not know. And on staying sane inside the noise: how to protect your attention from a media landscape built to farm it.

Join us for a conversation grounded in philosophy, insight and anecdotes drawn from a career spent observing radicalisation up close, made for anyone trying to stay curious in an age built to make us certain.
events.title: The Cult of the Internet

events.description:
Since the dawn of culture, philosophers, theologians, and social theorists have argued over the correct way to determine moral action. Is it based on reason, outcomes, or the word of God? Common to nearly all was the belief that there was a right answer. Churches, courts, and constitutions were built on the assumption that morality was discovered and not invented. But increasingly critics reject this outlook altogether. Competing accounts diverge so radically that no single theory can plausibly claim to be morally correct. Practices once upheld as moral are now condemned as barbaric. The Greeks thought slavery natural and just, Hitler described the holocaust as a 'moral imperative', and just a hundred years ago the US Supreme Court ruled forced sterilisation of the disabled a state obligation.

Should we abandon the idea that there is a correct way to determine good and evil? Do moral rules, codes and principles always result in perverse outcomes in some scenarios? Or is it essential to be able to call on a single principle to determine right action, and if so, what is it?

Critical race theorist Tommy Curry, controversial author of Gaza's Gravediggers Norman Finkelstein, and Labour life peer Thangam Debbonaire debate morality.
events.speakers: Tommy Curry, Norman Finkelstein, Thangam Debbonaire. Jay Shapiro hosts
events.title: The Code for Good and Evil

events.description:
Across the developed world, voters have been told to expect a permanent doom loop of high debt, low growth, and stagnant living standards. Join former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt, author of Can We Be Rich Again?, as he makes the unfashionable case for optimism. Drawing on his years inside government, Hunt argues that the solutions to our problems are within reach, that our strengths are consistently underrated, and that we are closer to a growth breakthrough than the gloom-mongers suggest.

“A fiercely intelligent and rich insider vision.” – Anthony Seldon
events.title: We Can Be Rich Again

events.description:
A handful of companies are racing to build machines that surpass human intelligence, and the economic shockwaves are already being felt. Some economists predict an explosion of growth; others warn of mass job losses and wealth concentrated in ever fewer hands. Two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist Sebastian Mallaby's recent biography of Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis gave him inside access to the minds and institutions creating the technology. Chief economics commentator at the Financial Times, Martin Wolf, argues this technology is changing our economies faster than we can manage. Join them to explore the latest in the pursuit of superintelligence, and the economic shifts that are inescapable for all of us.

“Martin Wolf is our wisest, most acute, and most experienced commentator." – Angus Deaton

"[Sebastian is] not just a marvelous writer. He's also a marvelous expositor." – Larry Kotlikoff
events.title: The Future of the AI Economy

events.description:
Join Joanna Moncrieff as she traces the history of mental distress – from its origins in supernatural explanation, to the emergence of biological and psychological models in the early 20th century, to the age of mass diagnosis and medication we inhabit today. Professor of Critical and Social Psychiatry at University College London and author of the landmark systematic review that upended the serotonin theory of depression, Moncrieff’s groundbreaking research makes the case for why medicine needs to develop a richer and more honest framework for understanding mental suffering.

Part 1: The History of Mental Distress: Mental distress through the ages: how the past continues to shape the way we think about the mind.

Part 2: Thinking Differently – A New Framework for Mental Health: Moncrieff looks beyond the chemical model to ask what a truly honest response to mental suffering might demand of us.

"Moncrieff explains both the scientific flaws and the deliberate manipulations underlying much of today’s psychiatric ideology and treatment." — Gabor Maté
events.title: The Misdiagnosed Mind: Depression Through The Ages

events.description: What if you found a magic potion called "Liquid Luck" that guaranteed you would win every game, ace every test, and never stub your toe again? Would you drink it? And if you did, would your wins still feel like they were really yours? Join philosopher Alexandra Konoplyanik to explore what makes someone lucky, whether you can create your own luck, and if it's ever possible to have too much good luck.
events.title: The Liquid Luck Potion

events.description:
With the hard problem of consciousness remaining unsolved, neuroscience is increasingly dismissed as unable to provide the answers we want. Join world-leading neuroscientists Mark Solms, author of The Hidden Spring, and Edward Bullmore, author of The Inflamed Mind, as they argue neuroscience does not go against philosophy and psychology. Rather, the philosophical and psychological insights of figures like Freud and Descartes can be supported or challenged through studies of the physical brain.

"Extraordinary on so many levels." – Brian Eno

“One of the world’s most accomplished and compassionate psychiatrists.” – Karl Friston
events.title: Freud, Descartes, and the Matter Behind the Mind

events.description:
Your opportunity to enjoy a delicious lunch with our inspiring speakers and award-winning wine.

Science cannot deliver a God's-eye view of reality. It never could. That's the argument of one of America's most provocative astrophysicists, Adam Frank, co-author of The Blind Spot. Join him to challenge one of science's most cherished illusions and explain why ignoring it is holding us back.

Click here to view the Lunch menu.

events.title: Philosophy Lunch with Adam Frank

events.description:
Most believe the US is no longer winning on the global stage. China has the largest military in the world and the largest navy, with the capacity to build warships at more than five times the rate of the US. China's economy has grown ten times as fast in the last thirty years and overtook the US in production capacity more than a decade ago. Even in tech, most analysts put China ahead in robotics and drones. While US alliances, once a key strength, now look precarious. But there's another side to this story. Half of the world's trade is still done in dollars. US military technology is supreme. While China faces a demographic time bomb threatening growth sufficiently for the OECD to forecast India as the world's largest economy in the 2060s, not China.

Is the US still winning the fight for global dominance? Has Trump's radical shift in foreign policy laid out in the 2025 Strategic Review hastened or halted US decline? Or is the very idea of winners and losers on the global stage a dangerous and profound mistake?

Joining us from Maryland, former US National Security Advisor John Bolton, former Foreign Secretary and Defence Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, and former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon debate American power.
events.speakers: John Bolton, Malcolm Rifkind, Nicola Sturgeon. John Prideaux hosts
events.title: Winning and Losing on the Global Stage

events.description:
The world is consumed with the power and potential of AI. Leading tech names like Altman and Musk have claimed it threatens humanity’s future. While trillions of dollars are being invested. The extraordinary success of Large Language Models, initiated by the breakthrough 2017 transformer/attention coding principles, is seen as just the beginning. More data, more computing, it is assumed, will deliver ever more powerful AI. But a growing number of critics argue these models are at root unintelligent word calculators that are reaching their peak as human training data is exhausted. To be intelligent, they would have to interact with the world, while language models merely find patterns in human text, predicting what comes next.

Does intelligence require an interface with the world akin to a human body, and is the future of AI in robots rather than chatbots? Is the belief that we can scale the attention paradigm profoundly misguided, and does it risk financial collapse as vast investments fail? Or will the language models become ever more effective and take over everything that humans can do?

"The next Einstein" Sabrina Pasterski, post-postmodern philosopher Hilary Lawson, Cambridge philosopher Audrey Borowski, and Oxford AI professor Michael Wooldridge debate whether AI will ever truly think.
events.speakers: Michael Wooldridge, Sabrina Pasterski, Hilary Lawson, Audrey Borowski. Güneş Taylor hosts
events.title: The Hype and The Limits of AI

Your opportunity to enjoy a delicious lunch with our inspiring speakers and award-winning wine.

The infrastructure of the surveillance state is being built right now, in plain sight. From ID cards to facial recognition to internet censorship, join the person who has fought every step of it, director of Big Brother Watch, Silkie Carlo, to debate the fight against tech surveillance.

events.description:
For generations, religion in the West has been in retreat. Recent claims of a "quiet revival" have been challenged, and in the US and UK regular churchgoing has fallen by more than 20% in a decade. In its place, many maintain the winning approach is to retain the values and even the trappings and traditions of Christianity, but jettison the metaphysical baggage. The renowned atheist Richard Dawkins declared himself a cultural Christian in 2024. Others like Douglas Murray and Jordan Peterson hold similar views. Echoing Tolstoy, who 150 years ago argued for abandoning the supernatural and keeping the ethics. But critics argue this settlement is incoherent. Without God, a cathedral is just a building, a ritual a superstition, and religious ethics a story.

Should we abandon cultural Christianity as an untenable compromise? Must we either eradicate Christianity's influence from our culture, or endorse it, including its supernatural beliefs? Or, in the face of social division, is it essential that we endorse its values, recognise it helped create Western beliefs in equality and justice, while rejecting its metaphysical claims as fantastical?

Orwell Prize-winning journalist David Aaronovitch, Reform UK figurehead Laila Cunningham, and theologian Alister McGrath debate cultural Christianity.
events.speakers: David Aaronovitch, Laila Cunningham, Alister McGrath. Jack Symes hosts
events.title: The Sacred and the Supernatural

events.description:
Bare Glazed Pottery Studio is a creative hub for budding artists and makers in Wiltshire! Join our portable pottery workshops for a fun and relaxing session of making. You will learn one of three different hand-building techniques; pinch pots, coiling or slab work and create a masterpiece that commemorates your wonderful festival experience. These workshops are structured around different levels of ability, so whether you’re a complete beginner or improver, all are welcome!

events.title: Pottery Extravaganza

events.description:
What is reality made of? How did the universe begin? Why does time only move forward? Physics a century ago was a place of intense discovery and progress. Today, there are many questions and few answers. Join CERN particle physicist Daniel Whiteson as he tours the biggest unsolved mysteries in physics, and asks how much closer we really are to answering them — or whether some questions may be unanswerable by design.

“It’s hard to imagine a more enjoyable way to explore the unknown.” – Sean Carroll
events.title: The Unanswered Questions Haunting Physics

events.description: 18 Nobel Prize winners come together to tell the universe's greatest story: how matter gave rise to life, and life to thought. They tackle humanity's most fundamental questions: what is the universe made of? Where does life come from? And how did it all begin?
events.title: Voices of the Universe

events.description:
For centuries, writers and novelists largely avoided putting themselves in their own stories and fictions. Shakespeare doesn't appear as a character in his plays. Nor does he write a play about his own life. The same is true for Austen, Hardy, Tolstoy or Hemingway. But today the fashion has reversed. Personal accounts, direct experience, are not only allowed but almost required by publishers and it would seem the public alike. Those that turn the lens inward to the self are gaining the applause of critics and culture and have become the winners of current writing style. But critics argue that the fashion for the personal is a mistake and reflects a shift toward an empty subjective relativism — there is no overall story, only 'my story'. And in doing so we are losing the universal stories and social patterns that have long anchored humanity.

Should we accept culture's obsession with the self as a true mirror onto lived reality? Or is it a narcissistic distortion that risks ending up with no shared reality at all?

The first female Odyssey translator, joining us from Pennsylvania, Emily Wilson, MacArthur-winning philosopher Rebecca Goldstein, and literary provocateur Patricia Lockwood debate ego and epics.
events.speakers: Rebecca Goldstein, Patricia Lockwood, Emily Wilson. Shahidha Bari hosts
events.title: The Ego vs The Epic

events.description:
Influenced by Plato's philosopher-kings and the Enlightenment's faith in reason, education has for centuries been regarded as the surest path to individual flourishing and collective progress. But today, the consensus is fracturing. Degree premiums are collapsing, and graduate unemployment is rising. Meanwhile, graduate debt is soaring, in the US surpassing $1.8 trillion. For many courses, the salary bounce is now less than the debt level. Moreover, AI threatens to automate the cognitive skills education is supposed to unlock. Nvidia's Jensen Huang calls for skills-based learning: “if you’re an electrician, a plumber, a carpenter — we’re going to need hundreds of thousands." Moreover, critics argue that in a Wikipedia age with knowledge available instantly to all, it is not the facts that matter, but the judgment and wisdom to choose between them.

Should we conclude that the educated are no longer winning, and that the future will favour the skilled and the self-taught? Should we take seriously Illich's argument that compulsory schooling manufactures conformity? Or should we not reject education itself, but an outdated conception of it that prizes facts over judgment?

Former senior cabinet member and Editor of The Spectator Michael Gove, Oxford economist Daniel Susskind, and Labour life peer Thangam Debbonaire debate the new world of education.
events.speakers: Daniel Susskind, Thangam Debbonaire, Michael Gove. Philip Collins hosts
events.title: The Rise and Fall of the Educated Elite

events.description: There once was a boy who absolutely hated every song he heard. One day, fed up with all the terrible tunes, he decided he'd write the perfect song. But his song didn't have notes, it didn't have any rhythm, and it didn't have a melody. In fact, it didn't have any noise at all! Join The Philosophy Foundation's Miriam Cohen to ask if silence can count as music. And in fact, what even is music at all?
events.title: The Music of Silence

events.description:
From Bill Gates' funding of research into reflecting solar radiation back into space, to Cornell University scientists' proposals to store carbon by burying forests underground, geoengineering is increasingly winning the case to be taken seriously as a response to the climate crisis. Once dismissed as fringe science, it is now debated in the pages of Nature, with tech optimists arguing human reason and technology give us the capacity and the obligation to actively manage planetary systems. But the risks are substantial. Harvard's solar geoengineering programme acknowledges that it could disrupt monsoon patterns, causing severe droughts affecting billions. And philosophers from Bruno Latour to John Gray have argued that the very idea of humanity mastering nature was always an Enlightenment delusion—one that got us into the crisis in the first place.

Should we abandon the idea that we can ever have dominion over nature? Should we reject geoengineering solutions to the climate crisis as deeply misguided? Or should we see geoengineering as a valuable and potentially vital response to radical climate change?

Editor of The BREAK-DOWN Adrienne Buller, astrophysicist Adam Frank, and award-winning researcher Laurie Laybourn debate geoengineering: promise and peril.

In partnership with SCRI
events.speakers: Adrienne Buller, Janos Pasztor, Adam Frank, Laurie Laybourn. Isabel Hilton hosts
events.title: Playing God with the Planet

events.description:
Most materialists treat consciousness as a mystery. Some of them think the only thing to do is to deny its existence. Others admit it’s real, and conclude that it ‘emerges’ from wholly and utterly non-conscious matter when that matter gets complicated enough (e.g. in our brains). Join the philosopher whose work revived interest in panpsychism, Galen Strawson, as he rejects the idea that such emergence is possible, and concludes that physical matter must have been conscious all along.

"A rare beacon of common sense in an ocean of intellectual eccentricity." – Philip Goff
events.title: The Physical World Is Conscious

events.description:
From the categories we use to organise society, to the institutions and practices that govern everyday life, the social world profoundly shapes who we are and what we can become. Sally Haslanger, Ford Professor of Philosophy and Women's and Gender Studies at MIT and author of the landmark book Resisting Reality, is one of the world’s leading philosophers of social structure. Haslanger traces how categories like gender and race are built and sustained by networks of practice and power – and how making those mechanisms visible is the crucial first step toward changing them.

Part 1: Gender, Race and the Architecture of Power: Haslanger examines how categories like gender and race materially organise and influence our practices, interactions and institutions as products of power rather than nature.

Part 2: How to Dismantle a Social Structure: Haslanger turns to the question of agency and transformation - asking how social structures can be challenged and dismantled.

"Haslanger is one of the very best analytic feminists in the country." — Society for Women in Philosophy
events.title: Gender, Race, and the Structures of Power

events.description: Two astronomers confront light pollution and join the dark-sky movement to establish Central Canada's first Dark Sky Preserve. Exposing the hidden cost of artificial light, this film reveals how it disrupts wildlife, damages ecosystems, and threatens human health.
events.title: Dark Skies: The Truth About Light Pollution

events.description: Taste is a gateway to how we perceive reality itself. Join philosopher and broadcaster Barry C. Smith, one of Britain's leading public intellectuals on perception and the senses. A regular on BBC Radio 4's The Kitchen Cabinet and Masterchef, Smith leads a wine-tasting where every glass becomes a philosophical revelation.
events.title: Wine Tasting and Philosophy with Barry C. Smith

events.description:
Liven up your afternoon with a glass of champagne, cake, and conversation with some of the world's leading thinkers.

We are overmedicalising misery, and it is making us sicker. That is the unflinching argument of one of psychiatry's most fearless internal critics, Joanna Moncrieff. A practising psychiatrist who has spent years dismantling the chemical imbalance theory of mental illness from within the field.

Click here to view the menu.

links.text: Click here to view the menu.

events.title: Champagne, Cake and Philosophy with Joanna Moncrieff

events.description: Imagine you come across a beautiful flowery meadow. But just before you can enter it, you hit a fence. "That's my meadow!" shouts an angry man. "I put that fence up yesterday because I want it all for myself!" Join The Philosophy Foundation's Matilda Atkins to ask if putting a fence around something magically makes it yours, and ask if anyone can truly own nature
events.title: Finders Keepers

events.description:
Darwin’s theory of evolution is our best explanation for life, but it has a well-known weakness: it cannot predict the future. It can only explain how we got here. In contrast, the big theories of physics, Relativity and Quantum Mechanics, make astonishingly accurate predictions, and so have long been regarded as science’s best theories, capturing reality’s deepest truths. Yet some philosophers, biologists, and even physicists argue that evolution may be the lasting winner, uncovering the universe’s ultimate nature. The cosmos, they claim, is not a mechanism governed by fixed laws, but something more like a self-creating, unpredictable organism, whose patterns are best explained by natural selection. Some physicists even argue that the laws of physics are not eternally fixed but rather have evolved through a process spanning multiple universes.

Can evolution dethrone the deterministic theories of Newton and Einstein as our deepest account of reality? Should we see the cosmos as an evolving, unpredictable flux, rather than a predictable, law-governed mechanism? Or is it ultimately governed by timeless laws that science should strive to uncover?

Stephen Hawking collaborator Thomas Hertog, CERN particle physicist Daniel Whiteson, and experimental quantum physicist Ivette Fuentes debate whether the universe evolves.
events.speakers: Thomas Hertog, Daniel Whiteson, Ivette Fuentes. Philip Ball hosts
events.title: Darwin's Physics and the Evolving Universe

events.description:
In the battle over how we should govern ourselves, the nation state has long been the clear winner, providing the law, defence and public services. But critics argue that the independence of the nation state is being challenged by the power of Big Tech. Amazon and Microsoft host over 60% of global government cloud data, controlling state infrastructure. Alphabet and Meta autonomously filter political discourse for three billion users, swinging elections without oversight. SpaceX’s Starlink unilaterally alters wartime communications, while Anthropic has vetoed US military use of their software in autonomous warfare. The global power of Big Tech makes it difficult or impossible for nations to tax heavily, fine, or break up these corporations. Increasingly, nations are instead choosing to partner with them.

Should we recognise that nations have already ceded power to Big Tech? And in doing so is the independence of nations itself at risk? Or, can nations wrest back control, banning social media platforms, choosing different vendors, and maintaining their monopoly over law and violence?

Former leader of Ireland Leo Varadkar, Big Brother Watch director Silkie Carlo, former senior cabinet minister Michael Gove, and Demis Hassabis biographer Sebastian Mallaby debate nations vs tech.
events.speakers: Silkie Carlo, Leo Varadkar, Sebastian Mallaby, Michael Gove. Roger Hearing hosts
events.title: The Nation State vs Big Tech

events.description:
The idea that the brain is the seat of the self and holds the key to the mystery of consciousness went unchallenged in mainstream thought for almost a century. But there are signs materialism is losing its grip — and so is the related assumption that reality reveals itself to human perception. In its place, some thinkers are returning to the idea of the soul to explain the self and consciousness. But critics argue this is repeating old mistakes. Join rising star and author of On the Memory of the Soul, Victoria Trumbull, and standard-bearer for post-analytic thinking who called time on linguistic realism, philosopher Hilary Lawson, as they ask whether the soul is a viable answer to an age that is moving beyond materialism.

“Hilary Lawson shows himself to be a latter-day 'metaphysician' on the grand scale.” – Alan Montefiore

“[Victoria’s] intricate study tackles fundamental questions about selfhood, identity and transcendence.” – John Cottingham
events.speakers: Hilary Lawson, Victoria Trumbull, Maria Balaska.
events.title: The Self, The Soul, and the Nature of Reality

events.description:
The West has lost its way. Its custodians, including its politicians, pundits, prophets, and priests, have failed. 200 years of global domination have been enjoyed, but only because the rest of the world was asleep. The rest have now woken up. Join the former President of the UN Security Council and author of Has China Won?, Kishore Mahbubani, as he argues for critical changes the West needs to make. If these changes are not made, Europe will become a museum and the US will become a self-absorbed country cut off from the world.

"Excellent and important." – Martin Wolf, FT
events.title: Five Fatal Fallacies of the West

events.description: Homer's Odyssey is among civilisation's oldest works of literature. With new excavations and jaw-dropping CGI from the studio behind Assassin's Creed, witness the world of The Odyssey brought to life like never before.
events.title: Ulysses: From Myth to Science

events.description:
Every fix for Western economies seems to demand the same trade-off: pain now for prosperity later, or prosperity now for pain later. Join former Conservative Chancellor Jeremy Hunt and the Labour Government’s Pensions Minister Torsten Bell as they debate across the political divide on which trade-offs are actually worth making. Spend or save? Cut or invest? Two men who've made these calls from inside government go head-to-head on the actual path forward.

"[Hunt is] someone who knows better than anyone how power is most effectively deployed." – Andy Haldane

"[Bell is] stellar: brilliant, incredibly pragmatic." – Rory Stewart
events.title: The Price of Economic Growth

events.description:
From the dawn of theatre in ancient Greece, we have looked for ways to entertain ourselves. Literature, art, films, the whole gamut of creative work devised to escape the mundane character of the everyday. As a result, we came to see the winners of life as those surrounded by excitement and stimulation. But in an internet age it is increasingly apparent that relentless stimulation may not be desirable after all. Boredom has quietly become a luxury commodity, as a 2.7 billion digital detox industry testifies. Neuroscientists have shown that the brain's Default Mode Network — essential for constructing our sense of self — is most active during wakeful rest. Constant stimulation suppresses it. Not surprising then that the wealthy escape with silent rural environments, and yoga detox retreats.

Should we embrace boredom as the route to a strong sense of self and a rich inner life? Should we see Big Tech as undermining our experience and our sense of who we are? Or should we be grateful for lives full of entertainment, once only available to a privileged few?

Hip-hop star and mental health advocate Jordan Stephens, fiction and nonfiction NYT 10 Best Books of the Year author Patricia Lockwood, and digital theorist Tony Sampson debate Big Tech and the self.
events.speakers: Patricia Lockwood, Jordan Stephens, Tony D. Sampson. Jay Shapiro hosts
events.title: Life, the Self, and the Infinite Scroll

events.description: In 1998, Nick Hayward filmed Australia's most creative songbird mimicking a chainsaw for Attenborough's The Life of Birds. Now he asks the question that has haunted him since: do lyrebirds imitate sounds of human origin in the wild?
events.title: The Message of the Lyrebird

events.description:
Four thousand years old, the Epic of Gilgamesh tells the tale of a search for eternal life. It is the oldest surviving literary epic, a thousand years before the Old Testament or Homer. The search for an elixir of youth, a Philosopher's Stone, has echoed through the centuries and across cultures. Chinese emperors died taking such potions, while the English King Charles II and Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf hastened their deaths. But these attempts were widely mocked. Even in the Gilgamesh story, the search for the elixir fails. The winning view has been that the search for immortality is no more than a fantastical goose chase. But many now claim that science can radically extend life. Mouse lifespans have been elongated 40% by removing 'senescent cells'. Some go as far as claiming that death itself could be permanently postponed.

Might ageing be a dIsease we can overcome? Are recent scientific studies evidence that life can be extended indefinitely? Or should we mock such claims as an ancient human desire that is not only impossible, but as Swift argued in Gulliver's Travels, is not even desirable?

Prophet of immortality, joining us from California, Bryan Johnson, longevity pioneer Aubrey de Grey, liberalism's greatest critic John Gray, and multi-NYT bestselling Sarah Wilson debate overcoming death.
events.speakers: Aubrey de Grey, Sarah Wilson, Bryan Johnson, John Gray. Güneş Taylor hosts
events.title: In Search of Immortality

events.description:
In the new multipolar world, we see the economic and military power blocks — the US and China, Europe and Russia - as the global winners dividing up the world between them. Trump's America is laying claim to the Western hemisphere. China is extending its influence along the old Silk Road and into Africa, while Russia is seeking to recapture the Soviet empire. But the story is less clear-cut. Iran and Ukraine have demonstrated the limitations of the great powers. Taiwan controls production of the world's most advanced semiconductors. Egypt, 30% of the world's container traffic. Nigeria will have the third-largest population in the world by 2050. India, the world's largest economy by 2060. Half the world's trade is outside the major power blocks.

Is the idea that superpowers rule the world a fairytale? Should we see in the fragmentation of power a world of danger? Or is a world with many sources of power one of potential and a shared future?

Former President of the UN Security Council Kishore Mahbubani, former Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng, and former leader of Ireland Leo Varadkar debate power and the multipolar world.
events.speakers: Kishore Mahbubani, Kwasi Kwarteng, Leo Varadkar. Mary Ann Sieghart hosts
events.title: Superpowers and Their Limits

events.description:
Gandhi’s philosophy of nonviolence appears beyond reproach: a selfless, universal politics of peace. Yet, what if this is deeply misleading? Join author of Gandhi and Philosophy, Delhi professor Divya Dwivedi, as she argues that beneath its apparent moral authority, Gandhi's thought not only failed to challenge the caste system, but actively upheld it. Drawing on a tradition of Indian dissent that stretches back to Ambedkar, Gandhi's low-caste political rival now revered in India, Dwivedi exposes how Gandhi's thought was an anti-politics that propped up a vicious hierarchy that condemned millions to permanent servitude and exploitation.

"A bold philosopher." – Meena Dhanda
events.title: The Real Gandhi Behind the Western Myth

events.description:
Gaza's destruction has raised urgent questions about the international institutions meant to prevent atrocities. Join Norman Finkelstein, one of the world’s most controversial scholars of Israel-Palestine and the son of Holocaust survivors, who claims the UN, international courts, and human rights bodies failed in Gaza. BBC journalist Roger Hearing sits down with Finkelstein to unpack the fierce arguments his work has provoked.

“An extraordinarily courageous individual who has paid a huge price for speaking truth to power." – John Mearsheimer
events.title: The Institutions That Failed Gaza

events.description: Under Trump's administration, tech titans including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Sam Altman have cultivated close ties with the White House. Driven by deeply libertarian ideas, how will this emerging alliance reshape the political landscape in the US and beyond?
events.title: Trump & The Tech Giants

events.description:
Most of us see punishment as a necessity, even as a moral good needed to prevent bad actors in society and rehabilitate wrongdoers. But what if the urge to punish has darker, more sinister roots? Join the philosopher working in prisons and inspiration for the BBC series Waiting for the Out, Andy West, to explore our instinct to punish and to challenge whether we are all as moral and good as we tend to think.

"Enriching, sobering and at times heartrending." – Lenny Henry
events.title: The Dangerous Urge To Punish

events.description:
A complete and overall account of ourselves and the world was once the goal of philosophy. But at the outset of the 20th century, Russell initiated analytic philosophy with an attack on overall systems in favour of piecemeal advance. Wittgenstein went further, denying even the possibility of an overall account. While at the close of the century, postmodernism declared the very idea of metaphysics naive. The case against a complete account of the world had seemingly won. But critics argue that from being over we cannot avoid the attempt to frame an overall account of the world. Any account of reality relies on a framework of belief to make sense of whatever is being claimed. We cannot eradicate metaphysics by simply avoiding talking about it.

Will grand philosophical systems make a return, and are they already doing so? Is it possible to navigate the world without an overall framework, and was there one underlying even postmodernism? Or is the idea of a complete account of the world a fantasy, born of hubris and pride?

Post-postmodern philosopher Hilary Lawson, revolutionary Indian philosopher Divya Dwivedi, and idealist philosopher Sebastian Rödl debate grand philosophical systems.
events.speakers: Hilary Lawson, Divya Dwivedi, Sebastian Rödl. Danielle Sands hosts
events.title: The Scaffolding of the World

events.description:
From drug treatment to therapy apps and wellness trackers, we believe we can intervene to improve our emotional and psychological well-being. Advocates of treatment have won out and largely silenced any opposition. In the UK, one in three women have been prescribed antidepressants. US spending on mental health treatment and wellbeing exceeds $700 billion. More than is spent on higher education. The counter view that emotional distress is not an illness to be cured, but a natural response to life's uncertainties, is dismissed as 'Victorian'. Yet record numbers are now suffering from depression and anxiety. Identified as the 'treatment-prevalence paradox', studies have shown that despite radical increases in treatment, there has been no improvement in mental illness.

Does the phrase 'mental health' already medicalise experience and undermine the variety of human response to circumstance? Have we created a mental health industrial complex that calls for ever more spending while failing to deliver well-being? Or should we be profoundly grateful to live in an era where treatments are available to alleviate mental distress?

Maverick psychiatrist Joanna Moncrieff, Freudian neuroscientist Mark Solms, neuropsychiatrist Edward Bullmore, and multi-NYT bestselling author Sarah Wilson debate the mental health industry.

In partnership with Big Think
events.speakers: Joanna Moncrieff, Edward Bullmore, Sarah Wilson, Mark Solms. Jonny Thomson hosts
events.title: The Mental Health Industrial Complex

events.description:
Economics claims to be a science, predicting markets and steering nations. Join economist and author of Debunking Economics, Steve Keen, as he argues the emperor has no clothes. Keen reveals how blind spots regarding private debt and credit creation caused the 2008 crash and will soon cause another, proving neoclassical models are fatally detached from reality. He attacks the discipline at its foundations, arguing that real economies are non-equilibrium systems driven by systemic instability. They are not self-correcting machines.

“No one is more qualified than Steve Keen to answer the question 'Can we avoid another financial crisis?'” – Yanis Varoufakis
events.title: The Lie At The Heart of Economics

events.description: The Ghazni marbles — 12th-century sculpted panels looted from Afghanistan — now sit across Western museums. But who do they really belong to, and can they ever go home? With Afghanistan's museums under Taliban rule, this film asks if restitution is even possible.
events.title: The Theft

events.description:
Funny Women finalist, part of the BBC Comedy Asian Network and listed in Dua Lipa’s ‘Service 95’ magazine as one of “5 new faces to know bringing a fresh perspective to the comedy scene”, Fathiya Saleh is hot off performances at Latitude Festival. She has since featured in the Comedy Queen’s sold‑out UK tour. Fathiya’s comedy offers her own cutting perspectives on topics exploring cultural identity and family dynamics, what it is like being one of the “girlies” and navigating the world as a young Muslim.

"An absolute delight." – Chortle
events.title: Fathiya Saleh

events.description:
Heidegger believed poetry, not philosophy, offers our best access to truth — that thinking must become more like poetic saying if it is to grasp what philosophy alone cannot reach. Join continental philosopher Babette Babich as she explores Heidegger's turn to Hölderlin and Rilke, but also what Anglophone poets can teach us that Heidegger's own thinking could not, and what it would mean to think — and to live — poetically once again.

"I like Babich's tough, at times even racy, rhetoric." – Clayton Koelb
events.title: Heidegger, Rilke, and the Limits of Language

events.description:
Fresh from shows at Glastonbury, Latitude, and Great Escape, and having earned coveted main support slots on major tours alongside indie titans Wet Leg and The Big Moon, Prima Queen are the next big thing and not one to miss. Included five BBC 6 Music playlisted singles, and their critically acclaimed debut EP, Not The Baby, earned praise from NME, The Guardian, and beyond. Not to be missed.

"Huge choruses. Irrepressible musical chemistry." – NME
events.title: Prima Queen

events.description: Only 25,000 polar bears are left in the wild. Trade Secret — from Executive Producer Adam McKay — follows a journalist, photographer, and advocate fighting to protect polar bears from commercial trade. But a disturbing truth emerges about those entrusted with saving the species.
events.title: Trade Secret

events.description:
Sexual liberation promised freedom from repression and taboo, and better sex for all. From the Kinsey reports to Cosmopolitan, Madonna to Sex and the City, the message was unanimous — the sexually liberated had won, the repressed were left behind. But critics argue this was misguided. While our openness has increased - what was once banned is often now seen as tame - the number of adults having sex at least once a week has fallen by a third since 1990. Nearly a quarter of young adults didn't have sex at all last year — double the rate from 2010. Bataille anticipated this outcome, arguing that eroticism requires transgression. Lacan insisted desire feeds on lack. Boundaries and prohibitions, they argue, are vital to erotic tension.

Should we conclude that prohibition and constraint are essential to desire? Do we need to reinstate limits and resurrect mystery to recapture intimacy? Or does this romanticise repression and risk returning us to a world where many did not enjoy sex at all?

Succession star and cultural provocateur Dasha Nekrasova, TikTok feminist firebrand Farha Khalidi, and director of Married to the Eiffel Tower Agnieszka Piotrowska debate prohibition as the engine of desire.
events.speakers: Dasha Nekrasova, Farha Khalidi, Agnieszka Piotrowska. Güneş Taylor hosts
events.title: The Architecture of Desire

events.description:
Festival favourites Alex Farrow and Chelsea Birkby return to HowTheLightGetsIn to wow audiences with their hilarious big-thinking comedy. Of course they are festival favourites, given that the world's largest philosophy and music festival naturally gravitates towards comedians who happen to be former philosophy teachers and philosophy graduates.

"An intelligent new star with a skill for strong joke writing." – Comedy.co.uk

"Sharp mind behind the sweet exterior." – ★★★★ Telegraph
events.title: Alex Farrow and Chelsea Birkby

events.description:
Lewis Garnham is a star comedian on the rise — "a gifted and spirited storyteller," raves Chortle (★★★★). His 2025 Australian tour sold out six cities outright, and his 22-night Melbourne International Comedy Festival run sold so fast he added 10 more shows — which also sold out instantly. The Scotsman (★★★★) calls him "a very natural, assured raconteur," while ArtsHub (★★★★) praises his "humorous connections and meaningful punchlines."

"Good. So good. Faultless." – Fringe World
events.title: Lewis Garnham

events.description:
Western nation-states, Reform's 2028 London mayoral candidate Laila Cunningham argues, have expanded far beyond their proper bounds — encroaching on citizens' freedoms in the name of safety, sustainability and public order. Join the Westminster City Councillor, former Crown Prosecution Service lawyer, and Reform UK politician as she makes the case against state overreach, from low-emission zones to housing and policing policy, and asks what it would take to roll back its reach and restore individual liberty.

“Laila is an enormously talented, successful woman." – Nigel Farage
events.title: The Tyranny of the State

events.description:
As seen on Amazon's Last One Laughing, Dave’s Hypothetical, ITV’s Hey Tracey, Comedy Central’s Roast Battle, and as a recurring guest on 8 out of 10 Cats Does Countdown and 8 Out of 10 Cats, Harriet Kemsley is a tour de force of the comedy world. She has starred in the Viceland reality sitcom Bobby and Harriet: Get Married, which she co-created and co-wrote with her husband Bobby Mair, to huge critical acclaim. Her other credits include hosting the BBC Radio 4 Comedy Club, The Radio 1 Comedy Lounge, BBC3’s Comedy Marathon, The One Show and Kevin Hart’s LOL Live.

"Reckless good fun. ★★★★" – The Guardian.
events.title: Harriet Kemsley

events.description:
With a spot on NME's 100 best British albums of all time list and rave reviews from Pitchfork, Rolling Stone, and even from Lady Gaga, Patrick Wolf made waves with hits like The Magic Position and The Days. This led to him being the first LGBT artist awarded the Burke Medal for Outstanding Contribution to the Arts. His sold-out Scala and Shepherd's Bush shows earned him the label of a visionary creator. Patrick joins us for a special one-off acoustic performance. Come and dance the night away.

“There’s nothing not awesome about him.” – Rolling Stone
events.title: Patrick Wolf (Acoustic)

events.description:
Cult cabaret royalty Bourgeois & Maurice (real names Liv Morris and George Heyworth) have spent almost two decades at the top of London's neo-cabaret scene. Since forming in 2007, the duo have staged multiple full-length theatre shows, released four studio albums, and won Best Music-Based Act at the London Cabaret Awards. Their 2016 Fringe show ranked among the top 20 best-reviewed comedy shows at Edinburgh that year, and they've twice taken Time Out's Alternative Eurovision title. Bourgeois & Maurice's work explores sex, politics, hedonism and the general absurdity of being alive, all wrapped in sequins and a very good key change.

★★★★★ – The Scotsman
events.title: Bourgeois & Maurice

events.description:
His clips have racked up over 100 million views online, and he has provided tour support for Stephen Bailey, Reuben Solo and Max Fosh. His split-bill Edinburgh Fringe show, Cold Brew Comedy, sold out across all four weekends of the festival. Alfie Dundas regularly performs at top comedy clubs across the UK, including The Comedy Store, Top Secret Comedy Club & The Frog and Bucket.

"Shows a lot of promise... I wouldn't be surprised if he goes far. ★★★★" – EdFringe Review
events.title: Alfie Dundas

events.description: For over twenty years, Leandro Silveira has lived with his wife, son, 20 jaguars, and other endangered animals at the Jaguar Institute he founded in the Brazilian savannah. With unique access, we follow the highs and lows of this wild family.
events.title: Wild Family: Living with Jaguars

events.description:
Appearing numerous times at the BBC, as well as at Glastonbury Festival and WOMEX, and collaborating and performing with projects such as Africa Express, The Turbans are an international collective whose music draws deeply from Arabic, Balkan, and Turkish traditions, with threads from Eastern Europe and the wider Mediterranean. Blending vibrant spontaneity, openness of spirit, and deep respect for one another’s traditions, the music speaks for itself.

"Highly danceable." – KLOF Mag
events.title: The Turbans

Start your day with a shot of inspiration from your favourite speakers. Expect stimulating ideas along with fresh pastries and coffee.

Why do we need our lives to mean something? It is not vanity or weakness. It is what makes us human. That is the argument of one of America's most celebrated philosopher-novelists, Rebecca Goldstein. Join the MacArthur Fellow and author of The Mattering Instinct to explore why mattering matters.

Join her to see the frontier of what we know about space, time, and reality itself.

events.description:
How did the political left stop fighting exploitation and start competing over who was most wounded by it? Join provocative cultural critic, professor and author of Virtue Hoarders and Traumatized, Catherine Liu, as she argues that our obsession with trauma has become capitalism’s greatest secret weapon. Exploring everything from the origins of PTSD to the era of Oprah, Liu criticises what the left has become from inside of it. The pathological belief that our wounds define us and that accommodating each other's suffering matters more than challenging power, she argues, has paralysed any real political action.

“One of the most courageous, brilliant, and radical thinkers in America today.” – Jennifer Silva
events.title: How the Left Weaponized Trauma

events.description:
Is physics a universal language, or a description of the cosmos shaped by the particular minds that produced it? Daniel Whiteson is Professor of Physics and Astronomy at UC Irvine, active researcher at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, and co-author of the acclaimed Do Aliens Speak Physics? Join Whiteson as he traces humanity’s journey to understand the universe – from the earliest Greek models of the cosmos to Einstein’s relativity – and how human physics might differ from the physics of other intelligent species. By comparing the two, Whiteson sheds light on the most fundamental question of science: whether our physics describes reality, or only ourselves.

Part 1: The Myth of the Universal Language: How mathematics and physics came to be regarded as the universal language of the cosmos.

Part 2: Rethinking Science, Perception, and Reality: Implications of the universality problem.

“Shows a way to think truly deeply about what physics is and how we come to learn about it.” — Sean Carroll
events.title: Alien Minds and the Universality of Physics

events.description:
For decades, cosmic inflation has been central to our account of cosmology — and the saviour of the Big Bang theory itself. The theory proposes that in the first microseconds of the universe it expanded 27 orders of magnitude in a tiny fraction of a second. Without it the Big Bang fails to explain the universe’s uniformity, the flatness of space, and the evenness of the cosmic microwave background radiation. But a growing and influential group of critics reject the theory altogether. We have no explanation for the force required to create cosmic inflation, nor for its coming to an end. Nobel prize-winning theoretical physicist Roger Penrose has gone so far as claiming that cosmic inflation 'has been falsified'.

Should we give up on cosmic inflation as a speculative theory constructed to overcome observations but which has no experimental support and fundamental theoretical flaws? If we abandon cosmic inflation, are there alternative accounts of the universe that we might uncover? Or is cosmic inflation essential to our whole account of the universe and one which we cannot afford to give up?

Nobel laureate, joining us from Oxford, Roger Penrose, physicist uncovering the origins of the universe Neil Turok, and TIME 100 astrophysicist Priya Natarajan debate cosmic inflation.
events.speakers: Neil Turok, Priya Natarajan, Roger Penrose. Hilary Lawson hosts
events.title: Cosmic Inflation and Cosmic Fantasy

events.description:
Advocating freedom is such a winning political strategy that every leader, from Xi Jinping to Donald Trump, Kim Jong Un to Vladimir Putin, claims to be in its pursuit. Every revolution is fought in its name. But, critics argue that the universal advocacy of freedom is evidence of its vacuity and its danger. The French Revolution's call for liberty ended in terror and mass execution. Stalin described the communist revolution as the first moment humanity was “really free”, while sending millions to the gulags. Mussolini wrote, “fascism stands for liberty, and for the only liberty worth having”. The idea of freedom begins to look less like humanity’s greatest achievement and more like its most dangerous delusion.

Should we conclude that the goal of freedom has always been an illusion? Are we wrong to treat freedom as an end in itself, rather than focus on other tangible interventions to improve our lives? Or, is the pursuit of freedom the most essential tool to fight tyranny and oppression?
events.speakers: Tommy Curry, Yaron Brook, Divya Dwivedi. Mary Ann Sieghart hosts
events.title: In the Name of Freedom

events.description:
Few know the gap between public image and private reality like Jordan Stephens. As one half of the hip-hop duo Rizzle Kicks and a bestselling author, he found fame young and has spoken openly about the pressures of performing a version of himself to the world. But his experience raises a question that now faces us all in the age of the curated online profile: if we are always performing a self, is there a "true" self underneath? Joined by Sarah Wilson, multi-New York Times bestselling author and social philosopher, Stephens asks whether a true self exists beneath the performance, or whether we are only ever the roles we play.

"Brutally honest as well as poetic." – Dolly Alderton

"Insightful and fiercely intelligent." – Julia Zemiro
events.title: The Philosophy and the Dangers of Fame

events.description:
The economy is working for some. It is very much not working for others. Join world-leading economist Mariana Mazzucato, who has gained honours from Italy, the UK, and even Pope Francis, and has held chair positions at the G20, WHO, and the UN. In this talk, Mazzucato proposes a new economics built around the common good. She argues that how we achieve our collective economic goals – through collective action, participation and reciprocity – matters just as much as what those goals are.

“Has at its heart a concern that all of humanity have access to land, lodging and labor." – Pope Francis
events.title: Capitalism and the Common Good

It's not every day you get to join a world-leading thinker for a delicious brunch. Avocado and eggs on toast never tasted so good.

Philosophy is often seen as a pursuit of the privileged. Yet the deepest questions about justice, identity, and meaning arise everywhere. Join focus of the BBC series Waiting for the Out, Andy West, who brings philosophical inquiry to prisoners, to explore freedom, purpose, and the examined life.

It's not every day you get to join a world-leading thinker for a delicious brunch. Avocado and eggs on toast never tasted so good.

Race, gender, and class are not facts of nature. They are structures built by power and sustained by ideology. So argues one of the world's leading social theorists and author of Resisting Reality, Sally Haslanger. Join her as she makes the case more rigorously than any other.

Click here to view the Brunch menu.

events.description:
Before Jimmy Wales founded Wikipedia, knowledge was gatekept by institutions, publishers and experts. His conviction — that knowledge should be freely available to everyone, and that people, given the right conditions of trust and good faith, will collectively pursue truth — produced the world's largest encyclopaedia and fundamentally changed how billions of people learn and understand the world. Two decades on, that conviction is under pressure. Misinformation is rampant, and AI systems, as Wales argues, produce authoritative-sounding falsehoods with no way for users to check them. Join Wales as he reflects on the philosophy and experiences that shaped one of the most consequential websites of our time and explores what Wikipedia's struggle for survival tells us about the future of truth and knowledge.

"Fascinating." – Stephen Fry
events.title: The Life and Philosophy of Jimmy Wales

events.description: When you visit a zoo and see a zebra, how do you know it's a zebra and not a cleverly painted donkey? Do you really know what you think you know? Or do you just believe in it? Join philosopher Steven Campbell-Harris to explore the mystery of knowledge. Puzzle over important questions about what we can be certain of in the company of other young, curious minds, and find out where your own extraordinary thinking takes you.
events.title: Donkeys in Disguise

events.description:
Physics is undergoing a revolution. The old idea of solid matter is losing ground, replaced by a new notion: information. Supported by Stephen Hawking's work on black holes, which suggests information is conserved even when physical matter is destroyed, many physicists now argue that information is the fundamental fabric of reality. But within this new orthodoxy, there is no agreement on what information actually is. The current winners are those who argue that information is physically encoded in quantum particles. Others contend the universe is a giant computer. Critics, however, argue that information is not physical at all but the means by which we construct our reality.

Should we see reality as information, and if so, how can a description of reality itself be reality? Or should we see information as a human invention, one born of our relationship to observation, data, language, and meaning? At root, is information the way we make sense of the world, or the very stuff of the universe?

Quantum physicist Ivette Fuentes, simulation theorist Melvin Vopson, astronomer Adam Frank, and CERN particle physicist Daniel Whiteson debate information and reality.
events.speakers: Ivette Fuentes, Melvin Vopson, Daniel Whiteson, Adam Frank. Bjorn Ekeberg hosts
events.title: The Reality Algorithm

events.description:
From job-hopping to open relationships, keeping your options open in life is often held up as a winning strategy. Across society, the markers of adulthood are being abandoned: job tenures for those at the start of their career have shrunk to just over a year, marriage rates are plummeting, and one in five adults have abandoned long-term goals altogether. Committing to a partner, career, or fixed set of beliefs is seen as the losing move — a surrender of personal freedom. But philosophers from Kant to Sartre warned that the endless deferral of real choices is nothing but a self-deception. A meaningful life requires commitment, not the illusion of infinite choice. The result of a culture that refuses to grow up isn't liberation; it's loneliness, burnout, and a mental health crisis.

Does genuine freedom require commitment, not the absence of it? Should we view the refusal to settle not as a lifestyle choice, but as a symptom of a deeper cultural crisis of meaning? Or is the idea of adulthood an illusion, and should we seek to remain forever young and open to all possibilities?

Heterodox sociologist Frank Furedi, radical journalist Laurie Penny, and FT columnist Jemima Kelly debate whether the refusal to grow up is liberation or a crisis of meaning.
events.speakers: Frank Furedi, Laurie Penny, Jemima Kelly. Jonny Thomson hosts
events.title: In Search of the Grown Up

events.description:
The West assumes modernity is its own invention, and that the rest of the world is simply catching up. Join one of China's most provocative and celebrated intellectuals, Wang Hui, as he argues otherwise. Tracing ideas that stretch back over a millennium, Wang contends China does not need to borrow modernity from the West. It has its own deep tradition of thinking about knowledge, power, and the good society — one that cannot be squeezed into Western categories.

“Consistently illuminating and bracing.” – Pankaj Mishra
events.title: China, the West, and the Myth of Modernity

events.description:
General relativity and quantum mechanics have stood for a century, yet they remain irreconcilable. Both Sabrina Pasterski and Neil Turok believe the answer lies not in adding complexity, but in radically rethinking our foundations. Described as the "next Einstein", Pasterski leads work on celestial holography: the idea that the physics of the familiar, four-dimensional universe can be captured by a hologram on the night sky. Turok, Higgs Chair of Theoretical Physics at Edinburgh, argues the Big Bang was not a beginning but a mirror, with a twin universe running backwards in time, making the Big Bang into a bridge between two universes, instead of a singularity. Join them as they set out their most radical ideas about the deepest mysteries in physics.

"Restlessly curious, brimming with difficult questions and bold new ideas." – Perimeter Institute

"I have been very impressed by his insight and originality." – Stephen Hawking
events.title: The Next Revolution in Physics

events.description:
Economics has long aspired to the precision and predictive power of physics. But can economics ever become a pure field of mathematical abstraction? According to Deirdre McCloskey, Isaiah Berlin Chair in Liberal Thought at the Cato Institute and author of twenty-five books, the answer is 'No'. Join McCloskey as she traces the story of how economics came to model itself on physics – and what has been lost in the process. She makes the case that economic life is irreducibly human, shaped by language, ethics and persuasion, and that a richer understanding of markets and society demands that we take those dimensions seriously.

Part 1: The Myth of the Mathematical Market: Economics as a predictive, value-free science - mechanisms and markets.

Part 2: Thinking Differently – Economics as a humanity: McCloskey makes the case for a different kind of economics - one that takes language, rhetoric, and ethics as forces that shape economic life.

"Persuasive…richly detailed and erudite." — Financial Times
events.title: Economics as a Human Enterprise

events.description: Imagine walking into a little shop with thousands of wonderful books! Out of the corner of your eye, you see a book with your name on the spine. You start reading, and it's the story of your life! Amazed, you keep reading until you reach the moment of standing in this very shop... Will you turn the page to see what happens next? Join The Philosophy Foundation's Zoe Drewitt to decide whether you want to know your future.
events.title: The Book of Life

events.description:
The historical record is unambiguous: every complex civilisation before ours has collapsed. Sarah Wilson - social philosopher, minimalist and multi-New York Times bestselling author – argues that ours is no exception, and that our studied refusal to reckon with this fact is precisely what makes the current moment so dangerous. Drawing on more than 200 conversations with philosophers, game theorists and spiritual leaders, Wilson offers not a counsel of despair but a rigorous, cross-disciplinary framework for navigating systemic breakdown with clarity, purpose and intellectual honesty.

"We need more people like Sarah alerting the world." – Alastair Campbell
events.title: A Civilisational Collapse Like Any Other

Quantum mechanics and gravity are the two great pillars of modern physics. No one has yet united them. A close collaborator of Roger Penrose, Ivette Fuentes is probing whether gravity itself collapses the quantum wavefunction. Join her at the frontier of physics.

events.description:
The manosphere has a simple story: feminism was a zero-sum game — women won, men lost. Its supporters claim progressive feminism is a power grab dressed up as progress. From diversity policies to #MeToo, they claim men are facing unfair treatment. This outlook is reshaping how a generation of young men see the world. Nearly a third of Gen Z men believe women should always obey their husbands. In response, critics argue the manosphere has misread the feminist project. Equality isn't a zero-sum game. A University of Notre Dame study shows increased gender equality leads to greater subjective well-being in both men and women. Whilst a 62-nation study found higher sexism correlated with lower productivity, more collective violence, and lower healthy lifespans for both genders.

Is it a mistake to dismiss the manosphere as self-evidently beyond the pale? Are there instances where gender equality has gone too far? Or is this a dangerous philosophy that should be buried — for even if equality did turn out to be a zero-sum game, what's wrong with that if it rectifies an existing disadvantage?

Hip-hop star and mental health advocate Jordan Stephens, critical race theorist Tommy Curry, TikTok feminist firebrand Farha Khalidi, and left-wing critic of the progressive elite Catherine Liu debate the manosphere.
events.speakers: Tommy Curry, Farha Khalidi, Jordan Stephens, Catherine Liu. Laura Kennedy hosts
events.title: Feminism and The Manosphere

events.description:
For at least the last century, democracy has been the undisputed winner. Not just as a political system, but as a moral creed. And remarkably, almost everyone claims it. From Western liberals to Chinese Communist Party officials, from the United Nations to the governments of North Korea and Iran, leaders present their systems as democratic, stage elections, and claim to invoke the people’s will. To question democracy is considered naïve or morally suspect. But today, a growing number reject the democratic ideal as a moral good altogether. We don’t consult the will of the people on technical problems in physics. Voting doesn’t guarantee the right outcome — the Nazis, after all, were democratically elected. And philosophers from Plato to Mill and Nietzsche have long considered rule by the majority no better than mob rule.

Should we abandon the idea that democracy is itself a moral good? Was Plato right that democracy is fundamentally flawed and always tends toward mob rule and demagoguery? Or is democracy an essential moral good which we abandon at our peril?

Libertarian thought leader Yaron Brook, Orwell Prize-winning journalist David Aaronovitch, pioneer of feminist social theory Sally Haslanger, and leading Chinese intellectual Wang Hui debate democracy.
events.speakers: Yaron Brook, David Aaronovitch, Sally Haslanger, Wang Hui. Isabel Hilton hosts
events.title: Democracy and Its Discontents

Your opportunity to enjoy a delicious lunch with our inspiring speakers and award-winning wine.

We assume we know what physical matter is. We are wrong. And that changes everything about consciousness. One of the world's most original and uncompromising thinkers on mind and reality, Galen Strawson, has spent his career making the case that physicalism doesn't escape panpsychism; it demands it.

events.title: Philosophy Lunch with Galen Strawson

events.description:
For much of the last century, culture waged a war on the merely pretty, instead favouring difficult, provocative art and architecture. But today, beauty is fighting back and winning. From government commissions mandating classical architecture to the algorithmic obsession with facial symmetry, a global return to beauty defined by order and tradition is underway. But at what cost? 90% of young women routinely alter their faces online, constructing a reality so perfect that actual faces feel like flaws. While in physics, some claim the hunger for elegant, "beautiful" theories has stalled progress, as researchers chase mathematical symmetry rather than inconvenient empirical facts. The result: an aesthetic built not on reality, but its avoidance.

Should we reject the new obsession with beauty as flight from the real rather than cultural progress? If we filter out every flaw and complication, do we risk a society so committed to aesthetics that it can no longer face the world as it is? Or is beauty embedded in reality and nature, and as a consequence both true and desirable?

Philosopher of beauty Heather Widdows, Succession star and cultural provocateur Dasha Nekrasova, and continental philosopher Babette Babich debate beauty and reality.
events.speakers: Heather Widdows, Dasha Nekrasova, Babette Babich. Jay Shapiro hosts
events.title: Too Beautiful To Be True

Bare Glazed Pottery Studio is a creative hub for budding artists and makers in Wiltshire! Join our portable pottery workshops for a fun and relaxing session of making. You will learn one of three different hand-building techniques; pinch pots, coiling or slab work and create a masterpiece that commemorates your wonderful festival experience.
